description:
HDFC Ergo vs Aditya Birla Health Insurance | Honest Comparison & Ratings | Beshak Insurance

If you’re buying health insurance in 2026 or choosing a health insurance plan for your family, this video helps you shortlist the best health insurance plan using real industry data-backed research. We have done a detailed health insurance comparison of Aditya Birla Activ One Max and HDFC Ergo Optima Secure, so you can decide what truly fits your needs in health insurance.
You’ll get a clear Optima Secure review, explaining the 2x Secure Benefit from Day 1, the Limitless add-on, and how its premium structure compares to other plans. Alongside this, we break down the Aditya Birla Activ One Max plan, covering Health Returns, Zero Premium Renewal benefits, the Sum Insured Multiplier, and the Unlimited Care add-on that provides lifetime protection.

We then compare core benefits like room rent rules, pre and post-hospitalisation cover, day care and domiciliary treatments, restore and bonus structures, and waiting periods including the 30-day clause, specified illnesses, and the 3-year pre-existing disease rule. Most importantly, we analyse real claim performance and service quality using verified data on settlement speed, complaint ratios, incurred claim ratio, rejection rates, and customer service audits, ensuring this HDFC Ergo vs Aditya Birla comparison is based on actual performance, not marketing claims — all reflected through Beshak Ratings.

comments.text: @beshak what if a person buys the insurance in a zone 2 or 3 and goes to a zone 1 for treatment is it covered or they can reject claim on the basis of zone?
comments.author: @pratikanand3025

comments.text:
Hi! In most cases, treatment in a higher zone (like Zone 1) is still covered even if the policy was bought in Zone 2 or 3. The insurer generally cannot reject the entire claim just because treatment was taken in another city or zone within India. However, a zone-based co-payment may apply depending on the policy terms.

In some plans, if you buy the policy from a Tier II/III city at a lower premium and later take treatment in a higher-cost city, the insurer may ask you to bear a part of the claim amount as co-payment. The percentage can vary depending on the insurer, the city of residence, and the city where treatment is taken.

That said, not all health insurance plans have zone-based co-payment clauses. So it’s important to check the policy wording carefully before buying.

comments.author: @fraziercastelino6550

comments.text: Hi!  If it was just occasional knee pain with no diagnosis, no treatment and no medical records before buying the policy, the insurer should not reject the claim due to non-disclosure of PED.  As per IRDAI, a Pre-existing Disease (PED) is one that was diagnosed by a doctor or for which medical advice or treatment was taken within 36 months before the policy start date. Anything older than this falls under medical history/other conditions, not PED. Medical history includes any past illness, surgery, conditions or major injury, even from childhood. That said, our view is always to disclose everything while buying insurance. Full disclosure avoids disputes later and keeps claims smoother and stress-free.

comments.text: Hi, that’s a very valid observation and you’re right to flag it. In this plan, the base structure is age-banded, which means the premium doesn’t increase every year, but only when you move to the next defined age slab. That said, age-banding doesn’t completely rule out other increases. Insurers can still revise premiums at a portfolio level due to factors like medical inflation, rising hospital costs, claims experience, or a revised pricing strategy. Age is not the only factor influencing premium. So while age is the primary driver here, long-term premiums can still change for reasons beyond just age, which is why looking at renewals from a long-term lens is important.

comments.text: What about claim settlement ratio of high value claims?
comments.author: @ashishjain962

comments.text: Hello! As presented in the video, the Claim Settlement Ratio by value measures the percentage of the total claim amount settled by an insurer against the total amount claimed, while the Claim Settlement Ratio by number looks at how many claims are settled out of the total claims received. An insurer can therefore show a high CSR by number if many smaller claims are approved, but still have a lower ratio by value if higher-value claims are scrutinised more closely or settled partially. This is why we show both metrics for better context. Also, as of now, there is no publicly available, insurer-wise IRDAI data that breaks claim settlement ratios specifically by high-value claims, since disclosures are limited to overall claim numbers and values, not claim-size buckets.
comments.author: @Beshak
